opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and it's one I think about a lot, because when you take continual learning seriously, really seriously, as in a system that's going to be learning for its entire lifetime in a world that's much bigger than it is, then a fixed architecture starts to look like a strange assumption.

Most of the time in machine learning we decide up front how big the network is, how many layers, how many units, and then we train it and freeze it. But if you think about an agent that's deployed, say a prosthetic arm attached to a person, or a system running in an industrial setting, it's going to encounter situations its designers never imagined. The world keeps changing, the person changes, the tasks change. So the question becomes: where does new representational capacity come from when the agent needs it?

One way I like to frame it is as a feature-finding problem. An agent should be able to propose new features, new ways of seeing its stream of experience, test whether they're useful, keep the ones that help it predict and control things better, and let go of the ones that don't. That's a generate-and-test loop, and it's very much in the spirit of work my colleagues and I in Alberta have been pursuing for years. You don't just adjust weights; you're also continually deciding what the structure itself should be.

And there's a practical motivation too. We've seen that deep networks trained continually can lose plasticity. They get worse at learning new things over time. Some units effectively die or become saturated and stop contributing. So growing, or refreshing, parts of the network, reinitializing units that aren't pulling their weight, adding capacity where it's needed, is one way to keep the system learning rather than ossifying.

The hard part is doing that in a principled way. When do you grow? What do you grow? How do you decide something is no longer useful when it might become useful again later? Those are open questions. But I think the direction is right: architecture shouldn't be something we hand to the agent once and walk away from. It should be something the agent participates in shaping, as part of its own ongoing experience.

r001.rationale: It contrasts adjusting weights with continually deciding and changing the network’s structure.

r002.rationale: It discusses adding capacity but does not propose starting from a single weight connecting one input to one output.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it sits right at the heart of what makes continual learning hard. The traditional picture of machine learning is that you fix the architecture up front, you decide how many layers and how many units, and then all the learning happens by adjusting the weights inside that fixed container. And that works beautifully when you have a well-defined problem and a dataset you can see all at once.

But continual learning isn't that. If you're an agent that's going to be running for weeks or months or years, in an environment that keeps changing, you don't actually know ahead of time what you're going to need to represent. The world is going to hand you things you didn't anticipate. So the question becomes: why would you commit, on day one, to the capacity and the structure you'll need on day one thousand?

The way I tend to frame it is that the architecture itself should be a learnable thing, not a fixed hyperparameter. Rich Sutton and I and others in Alberta have talked for a long time about this idea of generate and test. You have some process that proposes new features, new units, new little pieces of representation, and you have another process that keeps the ones that turn out to be useful and prunes the ones that aren't. The network is growing and shrinking in response to what the learner actually encounters. It's much closer to how we think about biological systems, where you have neurogenesis and synaptic pruning happening across a lifetime rather than a one-time build.

There are a few things I find really compelling about that. One is that it directly addresses the loss of plasticity problem that Shibhansh Dohare and others in our group have been documenting. If you keep training a fixed network on a non-stationary stream, over time units saturate, they become dead or dormant, and the network just loses its ability to learn new things. Being able to replace or add units is one of the cleanest ways to keep that plasticity alive. You're constantly refreshing the pool of things that can still learn.

The second thing is that growth gives you a natural handle on the stability-plasticity tradeoff. If you want to learn something new without overwriting something old, one option is to give the new thing somewhere new to live. You add capacity rather than fighting over the capacity you already have.

And then the third, which I think is a bit underappreciated, is that it changes what the learning problem even is. Instead of just asking "what weights should I have," you're asking "what should I be paying attention to, what should I be building representations of." That's a question about the structure of the agent's experience, and I think it's one that reinforcement learning is actually well suited to, because you can use the agent's own predictions and its own value signals to decide what's worth growing toward.

Now, I'll be honest that the practical side is still very much open. Deciding when to add a unit, what to connect it to, how to initialize it so it doesn't disrupt what's already there, how to decide when something has outlived its usefulness. Those are all hard. But I'd much rather be working on those questions than pretending the architecture is something we can get right once and then leave alone. For a learner that lives in the world, the shape of the learner has to be part of what gets learned.

r001.rationale: It contrasts adjusting weights inside a fixed architecture with treating the architecture as learnable and adding or pruning units.

r002.rationale: It discusses adding features and units, but does not propose starting from a single weight connecting one input to one output.

astra-6.text:
I think of the architecture as another thing the system can learn. In continual learning, the agent keeps having experiences, and those experiences may reveal that its current representation isn’t sufficient. So instead of assuming that we can specify all the capacity it will ever need at the outset, we can ask when it should add capacity and what that new capacity should do.

But growth by itself isn’t the goal. You could keep adding units every time something new happens, and eventually you’d have a very large system without necessarily having a better learner. The interesting question is whether adding structure helps the agent learn something it couldn’t learn before, while preserving useful things it already knows.

And I think that brings removal into the picture as well. What should we retain? What can we reuse? What is no longer useful? To me, growing a network is part of that broader problem of managing a representation over a lifetime, with limited computation and memory.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adding capacity and changing network structure, but it does not distinguish that from adapting weights within a fixed architecture.

r002.rationale: It does not propose starting from a single weight connecting one input to one output.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is: when does the system need more capacity? In continual learning, you have a stream of experience, and you don’t necessarily know ahead of time all the things you’ll need to represent. So growing the network is one way to give the learner room to develop new representations as its experience changes.

But adding neurons or connections isn’t, by itself, a solution to continual learning. You still have to decide what to preserve, what to change, and how to make use of that new capacity without disrupting useful things you’ve already learned. And you need to account for the cost. A system that keeps getting larger forever may not be a very practical lifelong learner.

So I’d think about growth alongside adaptation and reuse, and potentially pruning as well. Can the system recognize that its current representation is insufficient? Can it allocate additional resources where they actually improve its predictions or behavior? That makes architecture part of the learning problem, rather than something we specify once and assume will be appropriate for the rest of the system’s life.

r001.rationale: The response mentions growth alongside adaptation, but does not clearly distinguish changing weights within a fixed architecture from expanding the architecture.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose starting with a single weight connecting one input to one output.
